ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the London Bridge Research Ethics Committee in the UK (REC reference 17/LO/1480), the Comité de Protection des Personnes Nord Ouest IV in France (CPP reference 17/36) and the Medical Ethics Committee of Ghent University Hospital in Belgium (reference B670201836754).

In the Netherlands, the Medisch Ethische Toetsingscommissie Brabant waived the requirement for formal approval because the study was not subject to the Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act (reference NL62544.028.17).
The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
In the UK, the London Bridge Research Ethics Committee approved the study (REC reference 17/LO/1480), with Canterbury Christ Church University as sponsor.
In Belgium, the Medical Ethics Committee of Ghent University Hospital approved the study on 22 August 2018 (reference B670201836754).

In the Netherlands, the Medisch Ethische Toetsingscommissie Brabant confirmed on 20 July 2017 that the study was not subject to the Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act, and the requirement for formal approval was therefore waived (reference NL62544.028.17).
The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
All participants gave written informed consent before taking part.
All participants gave written informed consent before taking part.
In total, 605 participants were recruited across the UK (n=299), France (n=203), the Netherlands (n=55) and Belgium (n=48).

Alongside the core sessions, participants were signposted to optional "pick and mix" activities outside the formal programme, such as local gym sessions or yoga classes; some were free to participants (for example, walking groups set up in France), while others were at participants' own cost.

Patient-reported outcomes At each assessment point, participants completed validated measures of diabetes self-care (the primary outcome), physical and mental health, physical activity, illness perceptions, empowerment, eating behaviour and health-related quality of life.
Of 605 participants enrolled, 453 were assessed at the end of the programme and 293 at six-month follow-up.
Because participants were affected at different stages of their programme and to differing degrees between countries, the pandemic represents an unmeasured source of heterogeneity.

In Belgium, for example, participants were recruited largely through mutual health insurers (via their online and offline communication channels) and community health centres, often by a diabetes nurse rather than a GP.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

In the Netherlands, the Medisch Ethische Toetsingscommissie Brabant waived the requirement for formal approval because the study was not subject to the Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act (reference NL62544.028.17).
The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
In the UK, the London Bridge Research Ethics Committee approved the study (REC reference 17/LO/1480), with Canterbury Christ Church University as sponsor.
In Belgium, the Medical Ethics Committee of Ghent University Hospital approved the study on 22 August 2018 (reference B670201836754).

In the Netherlands, the Medisch Ethische Toetsingscommissie Brabant confirmed on 20 July 2017 that the study was not subject to the Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act, and the requirement for formal approval was therefore waived (reference NL62544.028.17).
live_data_statements: All participants gave written informed consent before taking part.
In total, 605 participants were recruited across the UK (n=299), France (n=203), the Netherlands (n=55) and Belgium (n=48).

Alongside the core sessions, participants were signposted to optional "pick and mix" activities outside the formal programme, such as local gym sessions or yoga classes; some were free to participants (for example, walking groups set up in France), while others were at participants' own cost.

Patient-reported outcomes At each assessment point, participants completed validated measures of diabetes self-care (the primary outcome), physical and mental health, physical activity, illness perceptions, empowerment, eating behaviour and health-related quality of life.
Of 605 participants enrolled, 453 were assessed at the end of the programme and 293 at six-month follow-up.
Because participants were affected at different stages of their programme and to differing degrees between countries, the pandemic represents an unmeasured source of heterogeneity.

In Belgium, for example, participants were recruited largely through mutual health insurers (via their online and offline communication channels) and community health centres, often by a diabetes nurse rather than a GP.
